title: "Math Cheatsheet"
description: "A refresher on the handful of math rules."
toc-depth: 3

You do **not** need heavy math for this course. But a few rules show up again and
again when we count steps and compare running times. Most of you learned these
years ago, so this page is a quick refresher.

You can also use [Desmos](https://www.desmos.com/calculator) to visualize the math formulas!


## 1. Exponents (powers)

$b^n$ means "multiply $b$ by itself $n$ times": $2^4 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 16$.

| Rule | In words | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $b^m \cdot b^n = b^{m+n}$ | Multiplying powers **adds** the exponents | $2^3 \cdot 2^4 = 2^7 = 128$ |
| $\dfrac{b^m}{b^n} = b^{m-n}$ | Dividing powers **subtracts** the exponents | $\dfrac{2^5}{2^2} = 2^3 = 8$ |
| $(b^m)^n = b^{mn}$ | A power of a power **multiplies** the exponents | $(2^3)^2 = 2^6 = 64$ |
| $b^0 = 1$ | Anything (except 0) to the power 0 is 1 | $7^0 = 1$ |
| $b^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{b^n}$ | A negative exponent means "one over" | $2^{-3} = \tfrac{1}{8}$ |
| $b^{1/2} = \sqrt{b}$ | A fractional exponent is a root | $9^{1/2} = 3$ |

**The one we use most.** Doubling the input of an exponential algorithm *squares*
its cost:

$$2^{2n} = (2^n)^2$$

So if $n = 10$ takes 1 second, $n = 20$ takes about $1024$ seconds, not 2 seconds.
That is why $O(2^n)$ is hopeless.

### Powers of 2, worth knowing by sight

| $n$ | 1 | 4 | 8 | 10 | 16 | 20 | 30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $2^n$ | 2 | 16 | 256 | 1,024 | 65,536 | ~1 million | ~1 billion |

## 2. Logarithms

A logarithm is just an exponent asked backwards.

$$\log_b x = y \quad\text{means exactly}\quad b^y = x$$

> "$\log_2 x$" reads as: **how many times do I have to double 1 to reach $x$?**
> Equivalently: **how many times can I halve $x$ before I get down to 1?**

$\log_2 8 = 3$ because $2^3 = 8$. And indeed $8 \to 4 \to 2 \to 1$ is 3 halvings.

That halving reading is the whole reason logs appear in this course: binary search
throws away half the list each step, so it finishes in about $\log_2 n$ steps.

| $n$ | 8 | 64 | 1,024 | 1 million | 1 billion |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\log_2 n$ | 3 | 6 | 10 | ~20 | ~30 |

Look at that last column: a **billion** items, and binary search needs only about
**30** steps.

### Log rules

| Rule | In words | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $\log_b(xy) = \log_b x + \log_b y$ | A product inside becomes a **sum** outside | $\log_2 (4 \cdot 8) = 2 + 3 = 5$ |
| $\log_b\!\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) = \log_b x - \log_b y$ | A quotient becomes a **difference** | $\log_2\!\left(\tfrac{16}{2}\right) = 4 - 1 = 3$ |
| $\log_b(x^k) = k \log_b x$ | An exponent inside comes out **in front** | $\log_2 (8^2) = 2 \cdot 3 = 6$ |
| $\log_b 1 = 0$ | You need 0 doublings to reach 1 | $\log_2 1 = 0$ |
| $\log_b b = 1$ | One doubling reaches $b$ | $\log_2 2 = 1$ |
| $b^{\log_b x} = x$ | Exponentials and logs undo each other | $2^{\log_2 5} = 5$ |
| $\log_b x = \dfrac{\log_c x}{\log_c b}$ | Change of base | $\log_2 x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 2}$ |


## 3. Adding up $1 + 2 + \dots + n$

This sum appears every time a nested loop skips the pairs it has already seen
(for example, checking every *pair* of riders once).

$$1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$$

**Why it works.** Write the sum forwards and backwards and add them column by column:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl}
S &=& 1 + 2 + \cdots + (n-1) + n \\
S &=& n + (n-1) + \cdots + 2 + 1 \\
\hline
2S &=& \underbrace{(n+1) + (n+1) + \cdots + (n+1)}_{n \text{ copies}} \;=\; n(n+1)
\end{array}
$$

So $S = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

**Example.** $1 + 2 + \cdots + 100 = \dfrac{100 \cdot 101}{2} = 5{,}050$.

**Why we care.** Expanding it gives $\dfrac{n^2 + n}{2}$ — the leading term is $n^2$,
so this sum is $O(n^2)$. A "half a nested loop" is still quadratic.

### Two relatives

| Sum | Formula | Big O |
|---|---|---|
| $\underbrace{c + c + \cdots + c}_{n \text{ times}}$ | $cn$ | $O(n)$ |
| $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + n$ | $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ | $O(n^2)$ |
| $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + \cdots + 2^k$ | $2^{k+1} - 1$ | dominated by the **last** term |

That last row is worth a second look: the whole sum is roughly *twice* its biggest
term. When a cost doubles each round, the final round alone accounts for about half
the total work.

## 4. Factorials

$n!$ ("n factorial") means $n \times (n-1) \times \cdots \times 2 \times 1$, with
$0! = 1$ by convention.

$$5! = 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 120$$

It counts **orderings**: the number of different ways to line up $n$ distinct things.
5 drivers can be visited in 120 different orders.

| $n$ | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $n!$ | 120 | 3.6 million | 1.3 trillion | $2.4 \times 10^{18}$ |

$n!$ grows faster than $2^n$, which grows faster than $n^2$. An $O(n!)$ algorithm
(like trying every possible route) is unusable past roughly $n = 12$.

### Choosing pairs and groups: $\binom{n}{k}$

$\binom{n}{k}$ (read "n choose k") is the number of ways to pick $k$ items out of $n$
when **order does not matter**:

$$\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$$

The case we actually use is $k = 2$ — the number of **pairs** you can form from $n$
things:

$$\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$$

With 5 riders there are $\tfrac{5 \cdot 4}{2} = 10$ rider pairs. Note the shape:
$\tfrac{n^2 - n}{2}$, again $O(n^2)$. Comparing everything with everything is
quadratic, whether you count it as a nested loop or as pairs.

## 5. Comparing growth rates

The single question Big O answers: **when the input doubles, what happens to the cost?**
Divide the cost at $2n$ by the cost at $n$ and simplify.

| Growth | $g(n)$ | Cost when $n$ doubles | Feels like |
|---|---|---|---|
| Constant | $1$ | same | instant, no matter the size |
| Logarithmic | $\log_2 n$ | **+1 step** | barely notices bigger input |
| Linear | $n$ | **2×** | twice the data, twice the wait |
| Linearithmic | $n \log_2 n$ | a bit over **2×** | good sorting |
| Quadratic | $n^2$ | **4×** | painful past a few thousand |
| Cubic | $n^3$ | **8×** | painful past a few hundred |
| Exponential | $2^n$ | **squared** | hopeless past ~30 |
| Factorial | $n!$ | worse still | hopeless past ~12 |

**The ordering to remember:**

$$1 \;<\; \log n \;<\; n \;<\; n \log n \;<\; n^2 \;<\; n^3 \;<\; 2^n \;<\; n!$$

In Big O we keep only the fastest-growing term and drop constants:

$$5n^2 + 100n + \log n + 3000 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad O(n^2)$$

The $100n$ term may well dominate for small $n$, but we are describing what happens
as $n$ gets large, and there $n^2$ wins.
